A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same GSE research. Their text, equations, tables and figures support reliable comparison. v1 ends with references; v2 includes Appendices A–E, containing both relocated material and additional experiments.

before.justification: v1 reports original attack-performance, runtime and interpretability results on CIFAR-10 and NIPS2017, including Tables 1–4 and Figure 4.

after.justification: v2 reports original results throughout Tables 1–7 and its interpretability plots, including additional ImageNet, classifier and adversarially trained network evaluations.

M1.justification: The algorithm retains the same quasinorm proximal updates, spatial adjustment of regularization coefficients, selected-coordinate subspace and projected NAG phase. v2 explains these as two explicit steps, but Algorithm 2 and the underlying objectives do not establish a changed procedure.

E1.justification: v1 actually evaluates CIFAR-10 and the NIPS2017 image collection, despite sometimes using the ImageNet label. v2 adds a separate ImageNet validation-set evaluation while retaining NIPS2017 in Appendix E.1. This substantially broadens the evaluated data, although targeted and untargeted image classification remain the tasks.

E2.justification: SAPF joins the Homotopy comparison in Table 1 and appears in additional comparisons. The explainability comparison replaces SAIF with comparisons involving PGD0, Sparse-RS and SAPF, as shown in Figures 2 and 5. StrAttack and FWnucl remain the principal benchmark comparators.

E3.justification: The CIFAR-10 untargeted sample count in Table 2 increases from 1,000 to 10,000, and v2 adds ViT_B_16, WideResNet and adversarially trained ResNet50 configurations. The reported CIFAR-10 step size changes from 0.0025 to 0.005, ACP changes to averaging successful attacks only, and runtime hardware changes from Tesla T4 to A40. These changes prevent treating the revised results as identical-setting comparisons.

E4.justification: Section 3.4.4 and Table 5 introduce a substantive robustness test against an adversarially trained ImageNet classifier, absent from v1. The explainability analysis also expands its comparison of structured and conventional sparse perturbations. The existing qualitative image examples are retained rather than newly added case studies.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, experimental seeds, confidence intervals, error bars or significance tests. Best, average and worst cases summarize target-label outcomes rather than repeated-run uncertainty.

E6.justification: Numerous results are revised or added. For example, CIFAR-10 ResNet20 average-targeted GSE ACP/d2,0 changes from 80.1/276 to 86.3/262; NIPS2017 VGG19 average-targeted d2,0 changes from 9704 to 11304. New results include 98.5% GSE success against the adversarially trained model and 94.8% average-targeted success on WideResNet. These are revised or newly reported outcomes under differing configurations, not established same-setting gains.

T1.justification: The formal ACP definition changes from averaging over all n attempted examples to the m successful examples in v2 Equation 15. The projected-NAG equivalence derivation is otherwise retained from v1 Section 2.4 in v2 Appendix C; its relocation does not constitute a new proof.

C1.justification: The central contribution remains efficient, group-wise sparse and explainable attacks. v2 explicitly strengthens the explainability contribution to superiority over both structured and traditional sparse attacks, while dropping the abstract and contribution-list assertion about maintaining lower perturbation magnitudes.

C2.justification: v2 explicitly characterizes first-stage coordinate selection as a heuristic and adds an interpretation of effectiveness against adversarially robust models. It removes v1's discussion of SAIF outperforming GSE at high saliency percentiles, while emphasizing group-wise sparsity's role in explainability. It also adds concrete explanations for excluding SAPF and Homotopy from further comparisons.

D1.justification: v2 supplies ResNet20 training details, pretrained-weight sources, the hyperparameter-search objective, runtime batch size and reported availability of ImageNet indices, target labels and grid-search code. These are substantial documentation additions, not proof that previously undocumented procedures changed. Conversely, v1's explicit Gaussian-kernel size of 5 and d2,0 patch size of 8 are no longer stated.

R1.justification: The structured-attack positioning remains, but v2 adds discussion of the already-cited SAPF work and references covering Sparse-RS, additional architectures and application areas. Optimization attribution shifts from Rockafellar/Nesterov to Li–Lin/Beck–Teboulle, and the dedicated SAIF discussion disappears. These refine and broaden the existing positioning.

P1.justification: v2 extensively rewrites and reorganizes the narrative: the method becomes an explicit two-step explanation, experimental setup is separated into datasets and attack configurations, and performance and explainability discussions are consolidated. Untargeted formulation, convolution details, the NAG proof and metric explanations move into appendices; social-impact discussion is incorporated into the conclusion.

P2.justification: Table 1 is reformatted into side-by-side targeted and untargeted blocks, additional robustness and appendix tables are introduced, and interpretability plots are redrawn with revised legends and panel arrangements. The existing untargeted illustration moves from Figure 2 to Figure 4, while the targeted examples remain Figure 3.

improvement.justification: The transformer and adversarially trained evaluations address applicability questions absent from v1, and the added training and data-selection documentation improves reproducibility. These benefits yield a positive but qualified improvement: v2 removes the adverse SAIF comparison from v1 Figure 4 and omits two previously specified parameters. Its stronger explainability claims and retained headline 100% success statement also insufficiently acknowledge the comparison gaps and lower success rates now reported in Tables 5 and 7.
